section.title: Woe to Ephraim and Jerusalem
section.sectionRationale: This opens the sequence of woes, chapters 28 to 33, that confront false trust, first in Ephraim's drunken pride, then in Jerusalem's scoffing leaders who have made a covenant with death. At its center stands one of Scripture's most quoted verses, the tested cornerstone laid in Zion, later applied directly to Christ in Romans 9 and 1 Peter 2.
section.thesis: The LORD who will trample Ephraim's fading crown of pride also confronts Jerusalem's scoffing rulers, who have made a covenant with death itself, promising instead a tested and precious cornerstone in Zion on which the one who believes will never be shaken.
section.frameNote: Four movements: woe to Ephraim's drunken, fading crown; the stumbling priests and prophets taught only line on line; the scoffers' covenant with death answered by the sure cornerstone; and the farmer's parable showing that even ordinary wisdom comes from the LORD.

verses.text: Woe to the majestic crown of Ephraim's drunkards, to the fading flower of his glorious splendor, set on the summit above the fertile valley, the pride of those overcome by wine.
Behold, the Lord has one who is strong and mighty. Like a hailstorm or destructive tempest, like a driving rain or flooding downpour, he will smash that crown to the ground.
The majestic crown of Ephraim's drunkards will be trampled underfoot.
The fading flower of his beautiful splendor, set on the summit above the fertile valley, will be like a ripe fig before the summer harvest: Whoever sees it will take it in his hand and swallow it.
On that day the LORD of Hosts will be a crown of glory, a diadem of splendor to the remnant of His people,
a spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and a strength to those who repel the onslaught at the gate.

units.label: Stumbling priests and prophets
units.note: line on line, precept on precept

verses.text: These also stagger from wine and stumble from strong drink: Priests and prophets reel from strong drink and are befuddled by wine. They stumble because of strong drink, muddled in their visions and stumbling in their judgments.
For all their tables are covered with vomit; there is not a place without filth.
Whom is He trying to teach? To whom is He explaining His message? To infants just weaned from milk? To babies removed from the breast?
For they hear: “Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there.”
Indeed, with mocking lips and foreign tongues, He will speak to this people
to whom He has said: “This is the place of rest, let the weary rest; this is the place of repose.” But they would not listen.

Then the word of the LORD to them will become: “Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there,” so that they will go stumbling backward and will be injured, ensnared, and captured.

units.label: The scoffers' covenant with death, and the sure cornerstone

verses.text: Therefore hear the word of the LORD, O scoffers who rule this people in Jerusalem.

For you said, “We have made a {{beritMavet|covenant with death}}; we have fashioned an agreement with Sheol. When the overwhelming scourge passes through it will not touch us, because we have made lies our refuge and falsehood our hiding place.”
So this is what the Lord GOD says: “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a {{ebenBochan|tested stone}}, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken.
I will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level. Hail will sweep away your refuge of lies, and water will flood your hiding place.
Your covenant with death will be dissolved, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand. When the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be trampled by it.
As often as it passes through, it will carry you away; it will sweep through morning after morning, by day and by night.” The understanding of this message will bring sheer terror.
Indeed, the bed is too short to stretch out on, and the blanket too small to wrap around you.
For the LORD will rise up as at Mount Perazim. He will rouse Himself as in the Valley of Gibeon, to do His work, His strange work, and to perform His task, His disturbing task.
So now, do not mock, or your shackles will become heavier. Indeed, I have heard from the Lord GOD of Hosts a decree of destruction against the whole land.

units.label: The farmer's parable of God's wisdom
units.note: ordinary skill comes from the LORD

verses.text: Listen and hear my voice. Pay attention and hear what I say.
Does the plowman plow for planting every day? Does he continuously loosen and harrow the soil?
When he has leveled its surface, does he not sow caraway and scatter cumin? He plants wheat in rows and barley in plots, and rye within its border.
For his God instructs and teaches him properly.
Surely caraway is not threshed with a sledge, and the wheel of a cart is not rolled over the cumin. But caraway is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod.
Grain for bread must be ground, but it is not endlessly threshed. Though the wheels of the cart roll over it, the horses do not crush it.
This also comes from the LORD of Hosts, who is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom.

beritMavet.gloss: A covenant with death, the scoffing rulers' boast that they had secured immunity from disaster through political scheming and deceit. The LORD answers this false covenant not with a rebuke alone but with an alternative, a real and sure foundation stone in Zion.

ebenBochan.gloss: A tested or tried stone, examined and proven reliable before being used as a cornerstone, the foundation piece that determines the whole structure's alignment. The New Testament applies this precise image to Christ, the stone the builders rejected who became the cornerstone, Romans 9:33, 1 Peter 2:6.

basic.context: This chapter opens Isaiah's sequence of woes with a taunt against Ephraim's drunken pride, her once-splendid crown soon to be trampled, before turning to Jerusalem's own scoffing leaders, whose spiritual drunkenness leaves them mocking the prophet's simple, repetitive teaching. At its heart the LORD exposes their trust in a boastful covenant with death and answers it with a far better foundation: a tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion.
basic.hermeneutics: Ephraim's judgment reflects real, imminent Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom, while the woe against Jerusalem's leaders addresses the same generation's arrogant political scheming, likely trust in Egyptian alliance, described as a covenant with death. The cornerstone promise, verse 16, functions in its own context as a promise of a secure foundation for those who trust the LORD rather than political maneuvering, while the New Testament reveals its fuller, messianic meaning in Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: Jerusalem's rulers boast of a berit mavet, a covenant with death, trusting lies and falsehood as their refuge. The LORD's answer employs even bochan, a tested stone, a term for a stone examined and proven reliable, the exact image later applied directly to Christ as the cornerstone in Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:6.
basic.typology: The tested cornerstone laid in Zion, on which the one who believes will never be shaken, is one of the Old Testament's clearest messianic images, directly identified with Christ in the New Testament as the stone the builders rejected that became the very cornerstone, quoted repeatedly of Him, Matthew 21:42, Acts 4:11, Romans 9:33, 1 Peter 2:6.
basic.christ: Isaiah's cornerstone, tested, precious, and sure, on which the one who believes will never be shaken, is quoted directly of Christ in Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:6, and Jesus applies the related stone imagery to Himself in Matthew 21:42. Where Jerusalem's leaders trusted a false covenant with death, Christ is the true and living foundation stone who alone secures those who believe in Him against the overwhelming scourge of final judgment.
basic.god: God exposes both drunken national pride and cynical political scheming as forms of the same underlying refusal to trust Him; He is patient enough to teach His people line upon line, yet just enough to let persistent mockery become their own trap. Even His judgment, His strange and disturbing work, serves His ultimate purpose of establishing a sure foundation for those who will believe.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 21:42-44 applies the rejected stone that became the cornerstone directly to Jesus. Romans 9:33 quotes Isaiah 28:16 to explain Israel's stumbling over Christ. 1 Peter 2:6-8 develops the cornerstone image fully, contrasting believers who trust the stone with those who stumble over it. 2 Samuel 5:20 and Joshua 10:10 record the historical battles at Perazim and Gibeon that verse 21 recalls.
basic.oneStory: This chapter exposes the futility of both drunken pride and cynical political trust, a covenant with death that cannot actually shelter anyone from judgment, and answers both with the promise of a sure and tested cornerstone in Zion. That cornerstone is Christ, the one foundation on which everyone who believes will never be shaken, however fiercely the storms of judgment sweep through.

context.literary:
Chapter 28 opens the run of woes that carries through chapter 33, and it is written with unusual craft. The first woe falls on Ephraim, the second on the leaders in Jerusalem, and the chapter is in effect a diptych, two halves that mirror each other. Both begin with drink and end with a crown or a cornerstone. In verses 1 to 4 a proud, garlanded city is likened to a flower fading and a ripe fig swallowed in one bite. In verses 7 to 8 the priests and prophets of Jerusalem are shown reeling in their own vomit. The cure for both is the same God, who becomes a 'crown of glory' for the remnant in verse 5 and lays a stone for the one who believes in verse 16.

The central section, verses 9 to 13, is a puzzle of voices. Verses 9 and 10 are the scoffers speaking, who sneer that Isaiah treats them like weaned babies, and the nursery chant that follows, whose syllables the BSB footnote says may be 'possibly meaningless sounds,' captures the mockery. Verses 11 to 13 then turn the mockery around. The same chant becomes God's word to them, spoken now in a foreign tongue. What they took for baby talk returns as the sound of invading soldiers.

The turning of words continues. The syllable that sneers at Isaiah's line in verse 10 returns in verse 17, where God makes justice 'the measuring line.' The scoffers' refuge of lies in verse 15 is swept away by hail in verse 17. Their 'covenant with death' in verse 15 is dissolved in verse 18. Every claim they make is overturned in the following verses.

The chapter closes with a change of key. Verses 23 to 29 are a parable in the style of the wisdom teachers, opened by a call to listen as in Proverbs, and its subject is the farmer. After four scenes of noise and threat the chapter ends in a calm field. The final line returns to the LORD of Hosts and calls Him wonderful in counsel, which gathers the whole chapter into a statement about divine wisdom.
context.historical:
Ephraim is the northern kingdom, whose capital Samaria stood on a hill that Omri had bought, 1 Kings 16:24, with a rich valley round it, which is the 'summit above the fertile valley' of verse 1. Amos describes the same elite in the same years, lounging on couches, drinking wine by the bowlful and failing to grieve over the ruin of Joseph, Amos 6:4-6. Samaria fell to Assyria after a three year siege in the sixth year of Hezekiah, 2 Kings 18:9-10. Verses 1 to 4 read as though they were spoken while the crown still stood, a warning to a city that did not listen.

The second half is addressed to Jerusalem's leaders in Hezekiah's reign. Assyria was the greatest power of the age, and the prophet's later chapters show Judah's court seeking help from Egypt, Isaiah 30:1-5 and 31:1. The Assyrian crisis eventually came in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, Isaiah 36:1. The 'overwhelming scourge' of verses 15 and 18 echoes Isaiah's earlier description of Assyria as a flood that would overflow its banks and sweep into Judah, Isaiah 8:7-8. The leaders thought they were safe because they had bought insurance.

The 'covenant with death' is a puzzle in its own right. It may describe a treaty with Egypt, which the leaders hoped would shield them from Assyria. Others note Isaiah's own warning against consulting the dead, Isaiah 8:19, and suggest an occult element, a pact with the powers of the underworld. The text does not choose. What it says is that the leaders were fashioning false refuges and calling them security.

The priests and prophets who staggered from wine were breaking a clear law, since priests were forbidden strong drink when they served, Leviticus 10:9, and other prophets had complained of preachers who would speak whatever the crowd wanted for wine, Micah 2:11. The farming scenes at the end belong to ordinary Judean life. Caraway and cumin were small seeds, beaten with a stick or rod, while grain was threshed with a sledge or a cart wheel.
context.canonical:
Isaiah returns to the themes of this chapter many times. He gives the first stone passage in Isaiah 8:14-15, where the LORD Himself is a sanctuary and also a stone of stumbling, a trap for the dwellers of Jerusalem. He gives an earlier warning of drunken leaders in Isaiah 5:11-12 and a similar picture of prophets in a stupor in Isaiah 29:9-10. His warnings against trusting Egypt come in chapters 30 and 31, and the call to stand firm in faith is in Isaiah 7:9.

The line that follows is taken up across the New Testament more than almost any other text in Isaiah. Jesus joins Psalm 118:22 to the image of the stone in Matthew 21:42-44 and Luke 20:17-18. Peter preaches it before the council, Acts 4:11, and quotes Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118 side by side in 1 Peter 2:6-8. Paul combines Isaiah 28:16 with Isaiah 8:14 in Romans 9:33, and in Romans 10:11 applies the promise that 'anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame.' He tells the Ephesians that the household of God is built 'with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone,' Ephesians 2:20, and the Corinthians that no one can lay another foundation than the one already laid, 1 Corinthians 3:11.

Verse 11 is cited in 1 Corinthians 14:21. Paul uses the line about strange tongues and foreign lips to say that tongues are a sign for unbelievers. The rest verse in 28:12 is taken up in the New Testament's account of rest in Christ, Matthew 11:28-30 and Hebrews 4:9-11. Verse 29 returns to the theme of wonderful counsel that first appeared in the name of the coming king, Isaiah 9:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted two audiences to see themselves. The northern kingdom was meant to hear that its beauty, built on drunken confidence, was already a fading flower. The southern leaders were meant to hear something harder, that they were doing the same thing in a sober suit. A people who cannot take God's word seriously will take refuge in a lie, and the lie, however clever, has no bottom.

He also meant to show that mockery of God's word is not neutral. The scoffers thought Isaiah's repeated, patient instruction was beneath them. The prophet's answer is that if they will not hear God in plain speech, they will hear Him in the speech of an invader, and the very repetition they scorned will become the rhythm of their capture.

The most important thing he meant them to grasp is the stone. In the midst of threat comes a promise that God Himself has laid a foundation, and that the one who believes will not panic. That was an invitation to Judah's leaders to drop the schemes and rest on God's own provision. Then the closing parable adds that God is no blunderer. He knows when to plough and when to sow, when to beat with a rod and when to spare the wheel, and His discipline is exactly the right amount for each grain.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records the words of scoffers and the answers of God, and it is important to keep them apart. The nursery chant of verse 10 is not a teaching method that Isaiah prescribes. The footnote suggests that it may be a mocking imitation, and the use of it in verse 13 shows God turning it back on those who sneered. The text does not tell teachers to teach in small units, though other parts of Scripture do value patience.

Nor does the chapter prescribe drunkenness or condemn wine in itself. What it condemns is leaders whose drinking leaves them unable to see or judge. Other texts handle the question of wine directly, such as Proverbs 20:1, and priests had a specific rule, Leviticus 10:9. The principle that carries forward is that those who guide others must be clear-headed.

The cornerstone is a promise, and it is given to be believed. The only imperative is quiet. 'Do not mock' in verse 22 is a warning to scoffers, and the farmer's parable is an invitation to trust a wise God, not a prescription for agricultural technique. Believers are meant to rest on the stone that God laid, not to build their own refuges, and to expect that He disciplines with wisdom.

debates.question: What does order on order, line on line, a little here, a little there, verses 10 and 13, actually describe: mocking imitation of Isaiah's simple teaching, or a genuine description of how God patiently teaches?

views.label: The scoffers' mocking imitation of Isaiah's simple style
views.case: The immediate context, drunken priests and prophets unable to handle solid teaching, suggests these are the scoffers' own words, mimicking and mocking Isaiah's supposedly simplistic, repetitive instruction as fit only for infants.

views.label: A genuine description of God's patient, incremental teaching method
views.case: The phrase's repetition in verse 13, describing how God's own word will come to them, suggests it may describe a real, patient pedagogical pattern that the scoffers rejected, turning what could have been gentle instruction into a trap because of their refusal to listen.

debates.bearing: Either reading agrees that the scoffers rejected simple, patient instruction from the LORD, and that their rejection, whether beginning as mockery of Isaiah's style or resistance to God's actual teaching method, turned the very words meant to instruct them into their downfall.

debates.question: Who or what is the stone in verse 16?

views.label: A person, the Messiah
views.case: The stone is laid by God, is precious, and is the object of faith: 'the one who believes will never be shaken.' The New Testament reads it of Christ without hesitation, Romans 9:33, 1 Peter 2:6. A believing relationship fits a person better than a building.

views.label: The Davidic house, Zion or the temple
views.case: In its setting the stone is laid 'in Zion,' and Judah's hope rested on the temple and the house of David. Some take it as the assurance that God's covenant with David and His dwelling on Zion would stand, with the faithful remnant as those who trust it, and see the Messiah as the final form of that promise.

views.label: God's own promise, or the faithful community
views.case: Some stress the metaphor of a foundation built into the life of a believing community, with faith in God's promise as the thing laid. They point to Isaiah 7:9, where standing firm is a matter of faith, and note that a group around the prophet's teaching was a sort of new foundation, Isaiah 8:16-17.

debates.bearing: These readings overlap, and the New Testament joins them. Christ is the person to whom the house of David and the dwelling on Zion point, and the community built on Him is the household of faith, Ephesians 2:19-22. The one thing every reading shares is that the foundation is God's gift, not a human construction.

debates.question: What is the 'covenant with death' of verse 15?

views.label: A political alliance, most likely with Egypt
views.case: The leaders wanted protection from the overwhelming scourge of Assyria, and Isaiah elsewhere condemns going down to Egypt for help, Isaiah 30:1-5, 31:1. On this view 'death' and 'Sheol' are Isaiah's biting names for an alliance that will bring the very ruin it was meant to prevent.

views.label: A pact with the powers of the underworld
views.case: The wording is close to the language of a treaty with Sheol, and Isaiah condemns consulting the dead, Isaiah 8:19. Canaanite religion knew a god of death. On this view some leaders may have turned to necromancy or other rites to ward off disaster, and the political scheming and the occult could be two sides of one trust in lies.

views.label: A figure of speech for presumption
views.case: Some read the language as the prophet's own ironic summary of their boast that judgment could not touch them. They never signed any such covenant. Their confidence in lies is a pact in effect, since they live as though death had agreed to leave them alone.

debates.bearing: The text speaks of the leaders' words and not of any particular signed treaty, and all three readings lead to the same point. Whatever they relied on, it was a refuge of lies, and the only real covenant with death will be the one that God dissolves, verse 18.

study.originalLanguages:
The nursery chant of verses 10 and 13, tsav latsav, tsav latsav, qav laqav, qav laqav, ze'er sham, ze'er sham, is the hardest line in the chapter. The BSB footnote renders it 'Do this, do that, a rule for this, a rule for that,' and adds that it may be meaningless sounds that show an inability to understand. The first word, tsav, can mean a command, and the second, qav, means a line or cord. What matters is the way the sounds are used. They are the monotone of a teacher heard by a drunkard, and then the same sounds come back in verse 17, where the word qav is the 'measuring line' God sets to justice. The scoffers' babble becomes God's plumb line.

The false refuge of verse 15 is machseh kazav, a refuge of lies. Machseh is the ordinary word for a shelter to run into, the word used for God as the 'refuge' of the poor in Isaiah 25:4. Judah's leaders have taken the vocabulary of God's protection and attached it to a lie. In verse 17 the same word returns, 'your refuge of lies,' as what the hail sweeps away. The overwhelming 'scourge' is shot, a word for a whip, and verse 15 pairs it with a word for flood. It is the language of a lash and a torrent together.

The promise of verse 16 turns on two words. 'The one who believes' is hamma'amin, from the root aman, the verb of Genesis 15:6 and of Isaiah 7:9, where Judah's king is told that if he does not stand firm in faith he will not stand at all. The Hebrew of 7:9 plays on one root twice, and verse 16 is that same root, now promising stability. The next verb, which the BSB renders 'never be shaken,' is literally 'will not hurry.' The Greek translation reads 'will not be put to shame,' and it is that wording that Paul and Peter quote, Romans 9:33, 1 Peter 2:6. The Hebrew picture is of one who does not rush off in panic, and the Greek picture is of one who is not disgraced. The two readings complement each other.

The word for scoffers in verse 14, letsim, is the word for those who sit in the 'seat of mockers' at Psalm 1:1. Proverbs 3:34 says God 'mocks the mockers,' and verse 22 is that principle at work: the one who mocks the word of the LORD finds his shackles heavier.

The 'strange work' of verse 21 uses two words for foreignness, zar, strange or alien, and nokhri, foreign. The people who mocked in 'foreign tongues' will find that God's own work is itself foreign to them, because it is God acting against His own people at places where He once fought for them. The 'decree of destruction' of verse 22 is the same sort of decree Isaiah 10:23 speaks of.

Finally, verse 26 says God teaches the farmer to do things 'properly,' and the Hebrew word is mishpat, justice, the very word used in verse 17 for the line. The verse 29 phrase 'wonderful in counsel' is a form of the verb behind pele, wonders, which stands in Isaiah 25:1 and in the name Wonderful Counselor, Isaiah 9:6, and 'excellent in wisdom' uses tushiyyah, the sound wisdom God stores up for the upright, Proverbs 2:7.

typology.type: The tested stone laid in Zion
typology.fulfillment: God lays a stone in Zion, tested and precious, on which the believer will not be shaken. The New Testament names the stone. Jesus asks the leaders about 'the stone the builders rejected,' Matthew 21:42, and Peter tells the council that this Jesus is that stone, Acts 4:11. Paul says believers are built 'with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone,' Ephesians 2:20, and that no other foundation can be laid, 1 Corinthians 3:11. Paul and Peter both set the stone beside Isaiah 8:14: it is a rock of stumbling to those who do not believe, and Jesus adds that it will crush the one on whom it falls, Luke 20:18. The type falls short because Isaiah's stone is not yet a person, and in Christ the foundation is also the Builder's Son.

Judah's leaders made a covenant with death, and God said it would be dissolved. In Christ the dissolving happens. Hosea had promised ransom from Sheol, Hosea 13:14, and Hebrews says Christ shared our humanity so that by His death He might destroy the one who holds the power of death and free those held in slavery by fear of it, Hebrews 2:14-15. The risen Lord says, 'I hold the keys of Death and of Hades,' Revelation 1:18. The escalation is that the covenant is not merely cancelled, but the one who holds the keys is a man who died and lives. The type is still unfolding, since death's last defeat is future, 1 Corinthians 15:26.

typology.type: The rest refused, 'This is the place of rest'
typology.fulfillment: God offered Judah a place of rest and repose, and they would not listen, verse 12. Isaiah 30:15 repeats the offer: in repentance and rest you would be saved. Jesus puts the offer in His own mouth, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28. Hebrews tells us that 'a Sabbath rest' remains for the people of God and urges us to make every effort to enter it, Hebrews 4:9-11. The correspondence is that rest is offered and can be refused. The escalation is that the rest is a person who receives the weary. The type is still unfolding, because the full rest is future.

typology.type: The overwhelming scourge and the sure foundation, an echo of the cross
typology.fulfillment: The scourge that passes through sweeps away every false refuge and leaves only the stone, verses 17 to 19. The Gospels do not cite this passage for the flogging of Jesus, so this is an echo, not a declared type. Still, Peter says of Christ that 'by His wounds you have been healed,' 1 Peter 2:24, and the stone on which Isaiah's scourge breaks is the stone who bore it. The pattern is that the one who believes shelters in the very place where judgment has fallen. It falls short as a one-to-one prediction because Isaiah's stone is laid before the storm, and Christ bore the storm Himself.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most directly through the stone. Isaiah says God Himself lays the stone, and it is tested, precious, a cornerstone and a sure foundation. The New Testament takes the verse as a statement about Jesus. Paul quotes it when he explains why many in Israel stumbled, Romans 9:33, and Peter quotes it when he tells believers that the stone is 'precious' to those who believe, 1 Peter 2:6-7. Jesus Himself fused it with Psalm 118:22 when He asked the leaders what was meant by 'the stone the builders rejected,' Matthew 21:42, and added a warning that anyone who falls on it will be broken and anyone on whom it falls will be crushed, Matthew 21:44 and Luke 20:17-18. Peter pressed it home before the council, 'This Jesus is the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone,' Acts 4:11.

The verse also shapes the New Testament's picture of the church. Paul says believers are 'built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone,' and that in Him the whole building becomes a holy temple, Ephesians 2:20-22. The tested stone is not only a security for individuals but the first piece of a new dwelling place for God. Its pairing with Isaiah 8:14 explains why the same person is a refuge to some and a stumbling block to others.

It leads to Christ through the covenant with death. The leaders thought they had bought immunity, and God said the pact would be dissolved. Jesus is the one who dissolves it, in the only way that would not be a bluff. He died, and He now holds the keys of Death and of Hades, Revelation 1:18, so that those who rest on Him do not have to make their own treaty. Hebrews 2:14-15 shows how: by His death He destroyed the one who holds the power of death and freed those enslaved by fear of it.

It leads to Christ in the offer of rest. The 'place of rest' that Judah would not enter is the rest that Jesus extends to the weary, Matthew 11:28-30. It leads to Him through verse 5, where the LORD of Hosts becomes a crown of glory for the remnant, since Peter promises that when the Chief Shepherd appears believers will receive 'the crown of glory that will never fade away,' 1 Peter 5:4, in contrast to the fading flower of Ephraim's crown. And it leads to Him through verse 17, where justice becomes the measuring line, since God has appointed a Man by whom He will judge the world in justice, Acts 17:31.

The caution is that Isaiah does not say the name. In his own setting the stone is a promise to Judah in the days of Assyria. The apostles read the verse in the light of the resurrection, and they are right to, but the original hearers were asked to trust a God who lays foundations, and that is the posture the verse still asks for.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who is both patient teacher and dangerous opponent of scoffing. He has said 'This is the place of rest,' verse 12, and He means it. The offer is the first thing He does. The judgment comes only because the offer was refused, 'But they would not listen.' This is the shape of divine anger in Scripture: it is preceded by invitation. The prophets rely on the point that God does not willingly bring affliction, Lamentations 3:33, and takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 18:23.

He is a God whose judgment is called a 'strange work,' verse 21. At Perazim and Gibeon He fought for Israel, 2 Samuel 5:20-21, Joshua 10:10-11, with a bursting flood and with hailstones. Now the same power is turned against His own people. That is why it is called His strange and disturbing task. Judgment on the covenant people is not what He prefers, but it is what holiness demands, and the reversal of Perazim shows that the covenant does not exempt them from the God of the covenant.

He is the God of justice as a measuring line. Verse 17 says He will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level, as a builder uses cord and plumb. Nothing in the building escapes that standard. A refuge of lies cannot be built plumb, and hail and water test every wall. In other places Scripture shows the same measuring line applied to Jerusalem and to Samaria, 2 Kings 21:13, Amos 7:7-8, so the verse is a warning that the standard is as strict for the leaders of God's people as it was for the nations.

He is the God who lays the foundation. The only active builder in verse 16 is the LORD, and the stone is His provision. The people who trust do not build their own shelter; they rest on one that has been laid. That is the gospel in miniature, a God who provides what He demands.

And He is the God of wonderful counsel and excellent wisdom, verse 29. The closing parable says that the farmer knows what to do because his God instructs him. If a plowman is taught the right measure of sowing and threshing, the Maker of the farmer is surely wise in how He deals with His people. The discipline of God is never wild. It has the care of someone who knows exactly how hard each seed can be beaten without being crushed.

In worship, the chapter calls for humility, the opposite of the scoffer's posture. Proverbs says God 'mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble,' Proverbs 3:34, and the verse is like a summary of the chapter's two halves.

crossReferences.note: Isaiah's earlier woe falls on those who rise early to chase strong drink and who 'disregard the actions of the LORD.' It names the same fault that Isaiah 28:7 charges against Jerusalem's priests and prophets: drink dulls the sense of what God is doing, and a leader who cannot see it cannot lead.

King Ahaz is told that if he does not stand firm in faith, he will not stand at all. The line plays on one Hebrew root twice. Isaiah 28:16 reuses that root in the promise to the one who believes, so the two verses together make faith the thing on which standing depends.

God is a sanctuary to some, but to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense. This is the other face of the stone of 28:16. Paul and Peter put the two verses together, so that the same stone is a foundation for the believer and an obstacle for those who do not believe.

God says that in repentance and rest the people would be saved and their strength would lie in quiet confidence, but they were not willing. It restates the rest of Isaiah 28:12 and shows that the refusal there was a settled habit of Judah's leaders, who preferred Egyptian horses to the Holy One.

God promises to stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line used against Samaria and the plumb line used against the house of Ahab. It shows that a measuring line is a standard of judgment, and that the standard applied to the northern kingdom would be applied to Jerusalem, as Isaiah 28:17 says.

David defeated the Philistines at Baal-perazim and said the LORD had burst out against his enemies like a bursting flood. Isaiah 28:21 names Mount Perazim to say the same bursting power will be turned on Jerusalem's leaders, a terrible reversal for those who had counted on God's old victories.

At Gibeon the LORD threw Israel's enemies into confusion and cast hailstones from the sky, so that more died from hail than from the sword. When Isaiah 28:17 says hail will sweep away the refuge of lies and verse 21 recalls Gibeon, the weather of Joshua's victory becomes the weather of Judah's judgment.

Paul quotes the 'strange tongues and foreign lips' of Isaiah 28:11 to say that tongues are a sign for unbelievers, not for believers. He treats the passage as an example of how an unfamiliar language can be a sign of judgment on those who will not listen to plain speech.

The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. Jesus joins this verse with Isaiah 28:16 in His teaching, so that the stone laid by God is also the stone that human builders threw away. The pairing explains how the one chosen as the foundation can be rejected by those in charge.

Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22 to the chief priests and elders after the parable of the tenants, and then adds that the one who falls on the stone will be broken and the one it falls on will be crushed. It carries the stumbling of Isaiah 28 and 8:14 into the teaching of Jesus about Himself.

Paul's quotation joins Isaiah 28:16 and 8:14, with the promise that the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame. He uses it to explain why Israel, pursuing righteousness by works, stumbled over the stone, and why Gentiles who believed found the foundation Israel missed.

Paul says believers are no longer strangers and foreigners but members of God's household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus as the cornerstone, a holy temple. Isaiah's single stone in Zion becomes the first piece of a living building.

Peter quotes Isaiah 28:16 and sets it beside Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 8:14, showing the stone from three sides: precious to those who believe, rejected by builders, and a cause of stumbling to those who disobey. The passage rests on the way Isaiah 28 holds a foundation and a stumbling block in one image.

Jesus offers rest to all who are weary and burdened, the rest He says will be found for the soul in His yoke. It is the offer Isaiah 28:12 describes as refused, and it answers the weary of that verse with a person who takes them in.

study.oneStory:
The chapter is another telling of an old story, in which people reach for a refuge of their own making and call it security. In Genesis the first shelter was fig leaves, and the first city was built by a man who ran from God. At Babel humanity set out to make a name with a tower. In Isaiah 28 the leaders of Jerusalem make a covenant with death and fashion an agreement with Sheol, and each time God does the same thing: He lets the false refuge be tested, and it fails. The lies that were meant to keep death out turn out to be the very things that death will pass through.

It also reaches back to the oldest sentence in the story. 'in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die' was God's word in Eden, and death came as the sentence on the human race. Judah's leaders think they can bargain with it. The Bible's answer is that there can be no bargain with death from our side, and that God Himself must dissolve its claim. The covenant with death is the human attempt at what only God can do.

Between the Testaments the stone passes from hand to hand. The prophet lays it in Zion, the psalmist remembers it as a rejected stone, the apostles identify it as Jesus, and the church becomes the building that grows from it. The same stone is a refuge for those who believe and a stumbling block for those who do not, Isaiah 8:14, which explains why the story of Israel's rejection and the Gentiles' welcome in Romans 9 uses the same verse.

The new creation completes it. The measuring line of justice is held by the One God has appointed, Acts 17:31, and every false refuge is tested. The place of rest that Judah refused is entered, Hebrews 4:9. The city in Revelation has foundations bearing the names of the apostles of the Lamb, Revelation 21:14, with the cornerstone that Isaiah said God would lay. 'The one who believes will never be shaken' is not a figure of speech at the end of the story but a description of the people who stand in the light and have no more fear of death, because the keys of Death and of Hades are in the hands of the Living One, Revelation 1:18.

quiz.q: What image describes Ephraim's coming downfall in verses 1 to 4?

options.text: A majestic but fading crown of pride, trampled underfoot like a ripe fig swallowed at first sight.
options.note: Verses 1 to 4 use exactly this image of a fading, easily consumed crown.

options.text: A fortress that successfully withstands every attack.
options.note: The opposite; the image is one of collapse and trampling, not successful defense.

options.text: A river overflowing its banks in blessing.
options.note: Not the image used here; the imagery is of a fading crown and trampled pride.

options.text: A vineyard that produces an unusually abundant harvest.
options.note: This vineyard image appears in a different Isaiah passage, not this specific oracle against Ephraim's pride.

quiz.q: Why does the LORD teach His people order on order, line on line, a little here, a little there?

options.text: Because the priests and prophets were spiritually stupefied by drink and could not handle more.
options.note: Verses 7 to 10 describe their drunken, muddled state as the context for this simple teaching style.

options.text: Because Israel's children were unusually gifted and needed advanced instruction.
options.note: The opposite; the simple style is connected to spiritual stupor, not advanced giftedness.

options.text: Because Isaiah had run out of things to say.
options.note: Not the reason given; the text ties this style to the audience's drunken incapacity.

options.text: Because foreign nations had banned complex teaching.
options.note: Not stated in the text; the explanation given relates to Israel's own spiritual stupor from wine.

quiz.q: What have Jerusalem's scoffing rulers boasted of making, according to verse 15?

options.text: A covenant with death and an agreement with Sheol.
options.note: Verse 15 states this boast explicitly and directly.

options.text: A covenant of peace with all the surrounding nations.
options.note: The opposite; their boast is specifically about escaping death and disaster through deceit, not general peace.

options.text: A new alliance with the priesthood.
options.note: Not mentioned in this verse; the boast concerns a covenant with death, not the priesthood.

options.text: A treaty to rebuild the temple.
options.note: Unrelated to this verse's actual content about a false covenant with death.

quiz.q: What does the LORD promise instead of the scoffers' covenant with death, in verse 16?

options.text: A tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion, on which the one who believes will never be shaken.
options.note: Verse 16 gives this exact promise, later quoted of Christ in the New Testament.

options.text: A new set of political alliances with Egypt.
options.note: The opposite of the point; the LORD offers a divine foundation, not another human alliance.

options.text: An immediate end to all future judgment.
options.note: The chapter continues to describe coming judgment even after this promise; the cornerstone is a secure foundation, not a cancellation of judgment altogether.

options.text: A promise that Jerusalem's walls will never be breached.
options.note: The promise given is specifically about a tested cornerstone and belief, not a guarantee about the city's walls.

quiz.q: What point does the farmer's parable in verses 23 to 29 make?

options.text: Even a farmer's practical wisdom in planting and threshing comes from God's own instruction.
options.note: Verses 26 and 29 state directly that this ordinary skill and wisdom comes from the LORD.

options.text: Farming is a purely human skill unrelated to God.
options.note: The opposite; the parable explicitly credits God as the source of the farmer's wisdom.

options.text: God punishes farmers who use different methods for different crops.
options.note: The parable actually commends this variation as wise, not something to be punished.

options.text: Farming should be avoided in favor of trusting God alone.
options.note: The parable does not counsel avoiding farming; it shows that even skillful practical work is itself a gift and instruction from God.

questions: Ephraim's crown of pride, though splendid, was fading and soon swallowed like a ripe fig. What source of pride in your own life might be more fragile than it currently feels?
The scoffers trusted a covenant with death, lies as their refuge. What lies or false securities might you be quietly resting on instead of trusting God's actual promises?
The cornerstone promise is that the one who believes will never be shaken. Where do you need that steady confidence right now, in a season that otherwise feels shaky?

The priests and prophets were too spiritually dulled by indulgence to receive more than simple, repeated instruction. Are there habits or indulgences in your own life that might be dulling your capacity to hear God clearly?
The farmer's ordinary wisdom in planting and threshing is credited to God's own instruction. Where in your daily work or skills might you be overlooking God's hand and provision?

translationNotes.note: Never be shaken can also be rendered will not act hastily or will not be ashamed, reflecting a range in how the Hebrew idiom is understood; the Septuagint's rendering, will not be put to shame, underlies Paul's quotation in Romans 9:33 and 10:11.

Mount Perazim and the Valley of Gibeon recall specific earlier battles, 2 Samuel 5:20 and Joshua 10:10, where the LORD fought for Israel against her enemies; here the same LORD rises to act, strangely, against His own people.

Order on order, line on line likely renders short, repetitive Hebrew syllables that may have mimicked either simplistic baby talk or a genuine teaching cadence, contributing to the debated tone of this phrase.
